key: creedence clearwater revival experience|have you ever seen the rain|151

track.title: Have You Ever Seen the Rain?
track.album: The Best of Clearwater Revival Experience

explanation.overall:
The verses say "I know" four times. The chorus says "I wanna know" six. That single swap is the song — a man who keeps insisting he understands what's happening to him, and a chorus that quietly admits he doesn't. He never lets the verse lines finish the thought either: each third line starts with that claim of knowledge and then trails into something unrhymed and unfinished (it's been coming, it can't stop, I wonder). The confidence is on the surface; the not-knowing is in the structure.

The music refuses to help him. Measured across the 30-second clip, the single most violent thing that happens is an energy dip of 0.08 — there is no drop, no build, no trapdoor. Energy sits in a narrow 0.31–0.46 band for most of the clip and the one peak, 0.64, arrives at clip 0:15 and is never approached again. A song about a storm coming gives you no storm. That flatness is the point: the arrangement stays at porch-level so the contradiction in the words has nowhere to hide behind a big moment.

What does move is smaller and stranger. Bar to bar the clip lurches between roughly 0.50 and 0.18 — near-full and near-third strength, about a bar apart at 125 BPM — so the groove rocks back and forth instead of pushing forward. And the top end steadily darkens over the clip's three thirds (2240 → 2027 → 1945 Hz). It gets warmer and heavier while the lyric gets bleaker. (This is a re-cut of Fogerty's 1971 arrangement; the measurements are of this performance, the writing craft is his — inferred.)

moments.what_happens: Energy alternates almost bar to bar: 0.53, then 0.23, then 0.50, then down to 0.18 here — the clip's lowest interior reading, roughly a third of the level a bar earlier. At 125 BPM a bar is about 1.9 seconds, so this is the arrangement emptying and refilling every couple of bars.
moments.why_it_hits: You feel a rocking, back-and-forth push rather than a drive. The song sways instead of charging, which is why a lyric about a storm coming still feels like something you'd hear from a chair on a porch.

moments.what_happens: Energy reaches 0.64 — the highest point anywhere in the 30 seconds — then immediately settles to 0.32 and never rises above 0.46 again for the rest of the clip.
moments.why_it_hits: The band's biggest moment is only slightly bigger than its average. Nothing swells to take the weight off the words, so the ache stays where it was put — in the sentence, not in the volume.

moments.what_happens: The largest interior change in the whole clip is here: energy slips from 0.71 to 0.63 — a drop of eight hundredths. Meanwhile the treble content falls steadily across the clip's thirds, 2240 to 2027 to 1945 Hz.
moments.why_it_hits: The mix quietly loses its brightness while nothing dramatic happens. The song darkens by degrees, the way a sky does — which is exactly what the lyric keeps describing and the arrangement never dramatizes.

moments.what_happens: Verse lines land 3 to 4 seconds apart. From the first chorus on, they land about 7.8 seconds apart — the words take twice as long per line while the band's tempo doesn't change at all.
moments.why_it_hits: The song decelerates without slowing down. He's been rattling through what he was told; now each word gets double the room, and you hear the question being asked slowly enough that it's actually a question.

moments.what_happens: The final chorus adds no new words — it's the second chorus again — and the last line delivered isn't the question but the picture: rain on a sunny day. The whole record is done inside two and a half minutes.
moments.why_it_hits: Nobody answers him. The song leaves you holding the impossible image instead of a resolution, and its shortness makes that feel less like an ending than like someone stopping mid-thought.

explanation.lyric_read: This is a lyric-first song and the writing is built on one contradiction held open for two and a half minutes: rain and sun at the same time, water that shines down. Tellingly, the rhymes are mostly slant and loose — "ago" against "storm," "before" against "hard," barely touching — except for one clean, locked couplet, and it's the one that states the impossible image ("so they say" / "a sunny day"). The one thing that rhymes perfectly is the one thing that can't happen. Then there's the hinge: every verse half's third line opens with "I know," and every one of those lines then fails to rhyme with anything and drifts off unfinished. He asserts, then trails. And the thing he claims to know is always secondhand — someone told him, so they say — while the chorus turns outward and asks you, six times, the one question the verses never answer. The song's real subject is the gap between being told how weather works and standing in it.
explanation.headline: Four times he says "I know"; then the chorus admits he wants to.

suggestions.title: Ain't No Sunshine
suggestions.why: Same device, pushed to an extreme: "I know" used as a repeated hinge where the speaker's certainty is the wound — Withers repeats it 26 straight times instead of writing the bridge.

suggestions.title: What's Going On
suggestions.why: A chorus that is a question aimed directly at the listener and deliberately left unanswered, with the arrangement staying warm and mid-level rather than swelling to resolve it.

suggestions.title: Free Fallin'
suggestions.why: The same rate trick: verse lines tick past quickly, then the chorus stretches one phrase across roughly double the space at an unchanged tempo, so the song feels like it slows while the band doesn't.
